utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies. Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Good day, General. Just to make sure that we're on the same page if we could just recap a little bit. Do you recall that yesterday we talked about your witness statement, paragraph 9, which says that you studied the combat reports and none of them report on such things as taking of identity documents, a tax on the civilian population, mass killings, deportation of the Albanian population, or deliberate destruction of religious and cultural buildings? Do you recall that we discussed that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to say good morning to everybody. Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And do you also recall that we discussed paragraph 20 of your witness statement which talks about the plans of the VJ and the VJ General Staff and states that there never has been a plan to support terror and violence against the Albanian civilian population in Kosovo, and I believe you also testified yesterday that there was no plan to expel the civilian population. Do you recall us discussing that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, but at the end of that quotation, which you summarised there, you made a mistake or there was a mistake in the translation. Anyway, I didn't put it that way. It doesn't say that in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Would you -- what I was stating was that -- and yesterday I believe I asked you a question if there was a plan, if your testimony was that there was no plan to expel the civilian population, and you agreed that there was no plan, but please state it in whatever way you believe is most accurate. Your testimony would be on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the problem, I did say that and I stand by that, but in that free interpretation of yours, towards the end you used an expression two words which I didn't actually say yesterday, so since it was rather long passage, I can't tell you exactly now, but we can take a look at it. Something about lending support, et cetera, et cetera. You said something and you used two words which I didn't use, and I'm sure you'll be able to find it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Was that about the expelling of the population or the violence against the population, which part of that did you have -- did you differ with, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd like somebody to read from the transcript in Serbian what it was and I'll then stop you, stop the person reading when he comes to that passage and then I'll say that's not what I said and that's not in the statement because I can't follow in Serbian otherwise. And as I say, it was rather a long passage that you read out, so I'd like us to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could go to yesterday's transcript, page 10824.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not yesterday, now, what you just read out now, the passage you read out earlier on a moment ago before you asked me the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So just to be clear about what I'm going through right now, sir. I just am trying to make sure that you recall the topics we discussed at the end of the day yesterday so that going forward we are both on the same page right now. So why don't I -- I'll try to simplify this by re-asking the question. Do you recall yesterday that we talked about paragraph 20 of your statement in which you say there was no plan to - and I'll read this - to support terror and violence against this Albanian civilian population; do you recall that we discussed that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that what it says there?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I believe that's what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like it to see the statement. That's what I'm saying. So that I can read it out loud, read out loud what it says there because that sentence does not stand either in the statement, nor did I say it yesterday, nor did I say it today, nor did I ever say to support terror against the civilian population. Perhaps it's a question of interpretation. I never said that we supported terror. I'll readily help you if I get the page so that I can read it slowly and then the interpreters can interpret it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: We can certainly put this up, sir, but you understand I'm not saying that you said there was a plan to support terror. I'm saying in your statement you say there was not a plan to support terror?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't use the word "terror." Throughout my statement all my testimony never did I use the word "terror."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I suggest that paragraph 20 in Serbian be put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. And this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Of Exhibit D553.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: 553. Thank you. If we could have paragraph 20, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Serbian, please, paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, General. So if we look at paragraph 20, you can read that --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: You can read that on your own in English. It says: "I solemnly declare that in the VJ and in the VJ General Staff there has never been a plan, order, or anything like that which planned, prompted, ordered or in any way assisted or supported terror and violence against the Albanian civilian population living in KiM." Do you recall that we discussed this paragraph yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that, but you left out a letter, the letter U, in the first sentence or perhaps the interpreter did, but it doesn't change the contents of what is being said, but I remember that we did discuss that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Sir, and finally I believe we also discussed that this last sentence that, the last two sentences: "No such plan could have existed without me knowing about it. Plans for the use of the VJ were drawn up and kept in the administration whose chief I was." Do you recall that we discussed that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct because all the plans that were devised were in the first administration and that's where they were stored and kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. So I think we are in the same place now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could now, please, pull up Defence Exhibit 160, D160.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, if we could have a look at a few parts of this and then I'm going to ask a question after we've looked at a few parts. If we look at the title of this, we can see it's Resolution 119, United Nations Resolution 119, and it's dated 23 September 1998. If we look down at the 6th paragraph down on the first page it starts with the words, "gravely concerned," and I'll just read this so that we have it in the record what we're --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: "Gravely concerned at the recent intense fighting in Kosovo and in particular the excessive and indiscriminate use of force by Serbian security forces and the Yugoslav Army which have resulted in numerous civilian casualties and, according to the estimate of the Secretary-General, the displacement of over 230.000 persons from their home." If we look at the paragraph just above it reads: "Noting further, the communication by the Prosecutor of the international Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia to the Contact Group on 7 July 1998, expressing the view that the situation in Kosovo represents an armed conflict within the terms of the mandate of the Tribunal." And if we look on page 3 in both the B/C/S and the English, it's paragraph 4(a) and (b), if you will just note there, sir, that this resolution demands that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia first cease all action by the security forces affecting the civilian population, and order the withdrawal of security units used for civilian repression, and (b) enable effective and continuous international monitoring in Kosovo by the European community monitoring mission and diplomatic missions accredited to the FRY. Now, sir, do you recall that this resolution was passed at this time in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't actually say that I remember, I wasn't in the General Staff at the time, and this didn't come within the frameworks of what I was interested in occupying my work post at that time within the job that I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So, sir, is your testimony today that you were not aware of this UN resolution that had such demands on the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. Maybe I did hear that the resolution was passed through the media, but I certainly didn't see it or read it, and I can't tell you much about it then.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So you were aware that it had been passed through the media? You'd heard about this in the media?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't informed of it through the media, but I heard that some such resolution existed, as did many others. I don't remember this one in particular or others for that matter except for the 244 one.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1244 one.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And General, in the summer of 1998, KDOM began monitoring the activities of the MUP, the VJ, and the KLA in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that either because in the summer of 1998 I had no points in common with Kosovo. I worked in the command of the 1st Army in Belgrade, and I didn't have occasion to follow that, nor can I confirm that now. But later on, I heard that this particular mission, KDOM, the American mission was an independent one and never was subordinated to the OSCE Mission. I happened to hear that somewhere later -- sometime later on when I arrived at the General Staff in January 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Is at some point before the NATO bombing, you were aware that there had been in KDOM monitoring mission, correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the he collegium, I heard somewhere that there was a KDOM mission before NATO executed the aggression against my country. But the details about its work and its general situation, I did not know and I don't know to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Fair to say though that the VJ was aware of KDOM. Maybe you personally didn't have detailed information but the VJ knew that KDOM was monitoring its activities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably. There were quite a few people in the Army of Yugoslavia whose job that was and who probably knew who was coming, how many people were coming in, and what their remit was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And then after the October Agreements in 1998, in late 1998, the Kosovo Verification Mission of the OSCE began monitoring the activities of the MUP, the VJ, and the KLA in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. Nobody monitored the KLA nor did they report on their evil deeds, not a single mission, not the OSCE and not KDOM either. Quite simply an agreement was not signed with them, I don't know why, and nobody controlled or monitored them at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: You will agree, sir, that the KVM monitored the activities of the VJ and the MUP? Leaving aside the KLA for now.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd leave MUP to one side because I know very little about that. And I do know that they monitored the units of the Army of Yugoslavia and the reason being is that we had observers who organised that part of the job, but what I want to tell you is this, I'm not really a good collocutor for this topic. It wasn't my area. I didn't follow it in any detail or studiously but just in a peripheral way when I happened to hear something, but my job involved something quite different, so I can't really say that I'm the proper witness for you to ask these questions of.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And, sir, that's fine, I'm really just asking not for details about it but just whether there is a general awareness that these existed, that KVM existed and was monitoring?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and to inform NATO or rather the American government directly. They did not submit reports to Walker, the head of the mission or his deputy, and that was common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, sir, at the time of the NATO bombing, so we are now talking March 1999 when this begins, this Tribunal, this Hague Tribunal existed, correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. We don't put it that way in my country. Everybody says NATO's aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia without a valid decision on the part of the Security Council, not campaign or bombing or whatever, and I don't know when the court started working, when the Tribunal was set up, when the decision was taken to set it up, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you if you are aware that this Tribunal existed in March of 1999, that it was in existence?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably it was, but I don't really know. I don't know when it came into existence and when the Security Council made a decision to form it, so I don't know the details, as I say. I can't remember. I would like to be able to answer your question, but I'm afraid I really can't. I'm not challenging the fact that it existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So just to get your testimony clear, you are saying that you are not sure in March of 1999 if there was a Tribunal that could prosecute war crimes in the former Yugoslavia, you weren't aware of that? Is that what you are saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that would be the proper answer, that I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. You recall yesterday we spoke about how you were aware there was an indictment and arrest warrant for Ratko Mladic from this Tribunal? Do you remember we talked about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And you agreed that there was an indictment and arrest warrant for Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that I agreed that there was such a thing. I agreed that I had heard somewhere, probably from the media, that that was in existence, and I say again, I did not see anything like that nor in a public -- nor was that published in our country except that warrant with the picture on the walls that he was being looked for, sought for, and that a reward would be offered for anybody, et cetera, et cetera, who could ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So in the years preceding the NATO intervention, there had been some high-profile indictments and arrest warrants from this Tribunal, Ratko Mladic, Radovan Karadzic. Is it your testimony you weren't aware that the Tribunal even existed by this time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not what I said. I said that I don't know when it was formed, when it started working, when it became operational.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm not asking you if you know the date that it first was formed. I'm asking you if you knew it was in existence by March 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just answered that question. I answered it twice this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you answer it again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What question was that? Was I aware that the Tribunal existed in March 1999? Is that it? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, as Resolution 1199 noted, which we just looked at, this Tribunal had made clear before the NATO intervention that the situation in Kosovo was within its mandate, meaning that it could prosecute any war crimes committed in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is what you said a moment ago and quoted earlier on, then it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Sir. Now, in your statement paragraph 18, you state and I'll just read from the statement: "I know" -- and this is, I'm sorry, Exhibit D553. "I know that in late April of 1999 General Ojdanic received a letter from the then-chief prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal Ms. Louise Arbour, and I know what action he took in this connection?"

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we can look at Exhibit 65 ter 00401.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the bottom of this letter, sir, you'll see that it's to Colonel-General Ojdanic, and it's from Louise Arbour Prosecutor. The date at the top if we could in Serbian just -- in the English show it's 26 March of 1999, but it appears in your statement you are saying that General Ojdanic did not receive this until later in April. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And if we could just look at this letter, in the first paragraph it says: "As you will be aware, the failure of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to co-operate with my office regarding the investigation of war crimes in Kosovo has been reported to the Tribunal's president to the Security Council of the United Nations." If we go to the next paragraph: "In that context and in light of current reports of escalating violence in Kosovo, I'm gravely concerned that serious violations of international humanitarian law continue to be committed." And the first sentence of the last paragraph: "It is my intention to investigate all serious violations of international humanitarian law that merit prosecution in the international forum, particularly those involving attacks on the civilian population." And if you look in the second paragraph it shows that the Prosecutor attached the relevant statutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, could I please tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be admitted as Exhibit Number P01525. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: If we could look at P01511.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And we can see from this that this same letter went to the president of Serbian, Mr. Milan Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And finally if we could look at P01513 already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: In this document P01513, we see that this same letter was also sent to Slobodan Milosevic, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So, sir, in light of these documents, would you agree that leading up to and during the NATO bombing, the VJ and the MUP had been the subject of a UN resolution; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that resolution that you mentioned a few moments ago, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes. They had been being monitored by KDOM and KVM?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And they were being scrutinized by this Tribunal in The Hague; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: This Tribunal in The Hague, the letters we just read from Louise Arbour, the Prosecutor at the Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The print is so small here of this text that I cannot see who they are actually after, and I kindly ask you to read that portion out of that paragraph, what you are claiming just now or enlarge the text for me. As for the other letters, I have not had occasion to see them until now. I see the 26th of March there and the aggression against my country started on the 24th of March. So this was allegedly written two days later, but it is stated in the log-book of the communications of the Chief of General Staff when communications arrived, and it's the end of April, so I can say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So, sir, you do recall this letter from the Prosecutor of this Tribunal going to General Ojdanic in late April? That's what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, except that now after so many years, I can no longer para-phrase it, but I do know that it did arrive, and I know that General Ojdanic was upset, was angry, because it was one month late because it went to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Justice and wherever else, and it's only then that it arrived in his office, and it was properly recorded that it arrived in his office, and I do know what measures he took after that. He informed his closest associates, his colleagues about that straightaway.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And, sir, you'll agree at this point the VJ is under scrutiny?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will not agree with you that it is the VJ that someone is after. Perhaps certain individuals are being -- are wanted because of the possible commission of war crimes. That is the the interpretation I received and that is not something I can agree with.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I'm not asking if anyone was wanted on charges. What I'm asking you is, will you agree the VJ was being watched by this Tribunal to see if war crimes would be committed?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How carefully this Tribunal watched this, I don't know, but there were verifiers on the ground, there were diplomats, there were intelligence officers who monitored that, and probably for the purposes of this Tribunal, they provided this information. That I do know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, sir, you'll agree with me that this letter that reached General Ojdanic says from Louise Arbour, "It is my intention to investigate all serious violations of international humanitarian law that merit prosecution?" You will agree the letter says that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that is what is written, then that's it. I haven't read it yet. I'm not challenging what you are saying right now, but I simply cannot see it here, I cannot read this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let me ask you this: If a combat report stated, "Today the VJ and the MUP went door to door through a village and expelled all the Albanians from their homes at gun point, on the way out of town we set the mosque on fire." If a report said that, that would be evidence of a war crime; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that is not written in a single one of our reports, not in a single one of the reports of the 3rd Army or our reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I understand you are saying it's not in any of the reports. Sir, if a VJ General Staff, if they wrote an order and that order said "Go from house to house and depart all the Albanians," that would be evidence of a war crime; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in that case, I would like to see that proof because the General Staff had never written any such thing or were they have written any such thing and that would be evidence if something like that did exist somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I understand you are saying it didn't exist, I'm asking you if a report like that would be evidence of a war crime, and I believe your answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was sitting and waiting but there were a lot of hypothetical questions here. What would have happened had this happened or what would have happened if things were this way or that way or some other way, calls for a lot of speculation and questions like that are being put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: General, in light of the scrutiny that the VJ was under, isn't this exactly the kind of thing that no one would put in a written report or order?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not right. Had that happened, that would have been written, and they would have to write it with full responsibility. It would have to be written by all the commanders from brigade level, corps level, army level, General Staff. We would not hide that. As a matter of fact, we would take measures against anyone who had done something like that so that they would be punished and properly prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, you'll agree it's not hidden if the leadership already knows very well that it's going on?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that once again, I did not understand, and it is a major problem for me is when you say at the very outset of your question you will agree. Could you please put that question to me very carefully once again so that I would answer it impeccably.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, you said that people would never leave this out of reports, they would never hide it from the leadership; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that, that is correct, and that is what I assert.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And I'm suggesting to you it's not hidden from the leadership when the leadership already knows that this is exactly what's going on, correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you know that, that the leadership knows that, then fine. But I do not know of our leadership knowing about that, and I assert that our leadership did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, in this trial, we've had a lot of evidence from witnesses who lived in Kosovo in various villages who were expelled from their homes by the VJ and the MUP. Is it your testimony that none of this happened?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not state that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Petersen. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Let us start from the very end, the last questions that were put to you. To the best of your knowledge in view of the position that you held, did the military organs take measures when they learned about misdeeds committed by their members?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you too. Yes, at all levels officers who were in charge of such matters did take measures and they prosecuted all of those who violated the law, especially international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is being insisted upon here that no one in his right mind would write up a plan saying let us expel a certain ethnic group, let us do something to a particular ethnic group. And now I am going to ask you, if there is not a plan, what about you and anyone else from the Army of Yugoslavia or the Republic of Serbia, did you carry out any kind of policy of persecution of the Albanian national minority during 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No plan, none of that. None of that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you now, if there was not a written plan, if there was a plan that had not been written up in the position that you held, would you have to know of such activity on the part of the Army of Yugoslavia or other security organs?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that is called a plan that can look like a plan regardless of whether it is in the form of text, map, or any other form, or quite simply any kind of assignment, any kind of note, no such thing was ever written, was ever compiled, because it would have to be preserved in special storage at the General Staff in the first administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In field reports, bearing in mind the system of reporting in the Army of Yugoslavia, did you receive any reports about planned and massive commission of crimes against the Albanian population or the expulsion of the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and if something like that had happened it would have been included in combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, if we could now explain the system of reporting from the very base, from the grass roots up to the General Staff headquarters during the war, could you explain this chain of reporting and filing reports, but briefly?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At lower levels it is oral, the commanding officer writes it up and then further up the regiment and the brigade they write reports every day on the basis of a certain structure as to what happened during the course of the day. When the corps collects these reports then they write up their own report and they send it to the army. When the army collects all of its reports they study them and they send a report to the Supreme Command staff, and the Supreme Command staff once they study all these reports they send their own combat report to the Supreme Command and then they act as I explained yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, no need to elaborate on this further. From January 1999 you were in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and you attended collegium meetings. Do you know who the members of the Kosovo Verification Mission were, professionally speaking, did you discuss that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. What was the name, the Kosovo Civilian Verification Mission? Yes, I know. For the most part or practically all of them, they were intelligence security officers from NATO countries who were trained and prepared to collect intelligence and information. They provided information through regular channels, but we are aware that they submitted other reports for the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the assessment of the General Staff, as it was at the time, tell me in terms of objectivity, how were these reports assessed?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we know and on the basis of the extent to which we could see this, we, I mean my colleague and I who worked on this, I could say that they were not fully objective and particularly they did not verify cease-fires on the part of the so-called KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Are you done?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, now, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to speak of the proportionality of use of force. To the best of your knowledge, from the beginning of 1999 that is, did you ever receive reports from the 3rd Army, daily reports?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until the beginning of the aggression we would receive daily operative reports and when the aggression started on the 24th of March, we would receive combat reports from the 3rd Army regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General, sir, do you happen to remember whether at the time when you arrived at the General Staff there was a team for co-operation with NATO and the KVM?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my superior. General Obradovic led the team in the General Staff and co-operated closely with the state commission or rather with the team in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the team, did it receive reports from the corresponding liaison teams from the 3rd Army and Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a regular basis, daily reports, weekly reports, so that they became acquainted with all the events on the ground with the support of the people who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, in the reports from the time you were in the General Staff, that is to say from the 13th of January until the beginning of the war, to the best of your knowledge, there was any disproportionate use of force by some units in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I never saw a report to that effect, and not only me personally, but the entire first administration scrutinized the reports in detail, and it was our duty to react if there was anything that was outside the system. But I'd like to add a sentence, nowhere did anybody in the world define what indiscriminate use or disproportionate use of force means. So just a digression. Now what was happening -- what is happening in the Middle East and what happened in the Middle East in other countries where NATO launched an aggression wasn't the greatest indiscriminate use of force when 19 of the strongest countries in NATO carry out an aggression without a Security Council decision on a small country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to ask you something else. Did you ever receive a report saying that any action on the part of the army or other security forces were directed against civilians in Kosovo and Metohija during 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with full responsibility that we never received a single report to that effect saying that army unit undertook any action against civilians in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, my colleague, the Prosecutor showed us Ms. Arbour's letter, and you explained to us that it reached the Chief of the General Staff at the end of April because of some difficulties in being handed over, but you interrupted when you were saying what the Chief of the General Staff did upon reception of the letter?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of the General Staff, or rather, the staff -- the Supreme Command staff gathered together his associates and gave him a task of reading the letter carefully, lawyers and other experts, to tell him what should be done, what he should do, and they proposed, and he had a similar idea, that he should send a telegram straightaway to General Pavkovic, the commander of the 3rd Army and to send him the letter too, and he demanded that he state his views on the letter and each section of the letter in very clear terms. Then he also requested that the 3rd Army commander in a written report with a dead-line should write down what measures he took on the basis of our orders and his orders to prevent war crimes from happening and when the dead-line was up, General Pavkovic did send in this detailed report describing all the orders and commands that appeared from the General Staff in the general army to show that he had received them and studied them as well as his own orders following on from those first orders so other orders too that he wrote at his own initiative to prevent war crimes which are now being discussed here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the reports that you received, was there any knowledge and awareness of civilians being persecuted or any organised crimes being committed against them or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no such case recorded in a written report by the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, according to the reports that you received, what about the individuals who did commit crimes, were steps taken to prosecute by the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and at one point in time during the aggression, the Chief of the Supreme Command staff issued an order that within the frameworks of a daily report, the legislative organs should provide precise data on a daily basis what they did in the area. So we could have a daily overview of how many prosecutions were executed, how many people were sentenced, tried, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we get D006-0042, please. The next exhibit. D557 is the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Section 4 in your set, General. Number 4, General. It's a response from the 3rd Army of the 21st of January, 1990, well, there is a mistake here, it should read 1999. Maybe it's not a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the translation says 1995 too, Your Honours, but it's actually 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you first, with infantry weaponry, automatic rifles specifically, are there or can they be -- can Tromblon mines and others be used against armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Rifle grenades and they are devices against armoured units, right, and when they are used they are considered to be fired from artillery weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's look at point 2. When regular training is carried out around the village of Rance to 700 metres west, fire was open from artillery weapons, and can you tell us which weapons were used by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it says here in this report, in addition to what you have just said, it says, and hand-grenades and from the village of Rance mortar fire, and it doesn't say which calibre or rather hand-held rocket-launcher, but it doesn't say whether they were 80 millimetre or 120 millimetre, but they were certainly mortar fire, so mortars were used, hand-held launchers were used and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, that's page 2 of the English, and it's towards the end of the first page in your set says from the village of Belince 700 metres south artillery fire was used, et cetera. Could you tell us what the rest of that is?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Belince is a 12/7 millimetre anti-aircraft machine-gun. It has various effects, inflammatory and so on, but it's considered to be a heavy machine-gun in the west, and the 82-millimetre mortar. Now, this defines quite precisely that 82-millimetre mortar was used to open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, may we have the next document called up, please, P1522.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I stop you here for a moment. On the second page of the telegram here, we have what we were discussing yesterday but did not actually see yesterday, and that is the following: A stamp when this telegram was received and a registered and the registration number in the General Staff. So apart from the other data that is usually there, here we see that the first administration of the General Staff on the 22nd of January received this particular telegram and entered it in the log-book under the number there, and it was signed by the colonel who was on duty. And what's more, in the lower left-hand corner, he wrote who it was being sent to so that there is a lasting trace as to what happened with this telegram and proof that it reached the General Staff, that it arrived in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General, we are going to look at P1522 now, please. Yesterday the Prosecution presented an order, showed us an order from the General Staff dated the 6th of March, 1999 sent to the command of the 2nd and 3rd Armies, and you were also shown item 1 of that order resubordination of the 3rd Army -- of the 37th Motorised Brigade on the 2nd Army to the 3rd Army Command. Now, could you comment on the following paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we zoom into that, please. Paragraph 2 of item 1. Item 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'll read it out, General. It says, "Resubordinations to be carried out in the garrison of the Raska peacetime location on the 7th of March." What does that mean, General?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that the unit which is being resubordinated must be ready and that a commanding officer or team would be arriving from the 3rd Army to which it is being resubordinated to see whether that particular unit is ready to carry out its assignment. The unit remains in its barracks on that territory until it receives permission to move on, move elsewhere. Now, the commander, or rather the team he sent establishes whether the unit is ready to carry out its assignment. From that moment, it is considered to be resubordinated to the commander of the 3rd Army or to whom he resubordinates it and carries out his plans and orders. And reports are sent out to two persons, to the 3rd Army commander or the Pristina Corps, resubordinated to it, and the exactly the same report is sent to the commander of the 2nd Army or rather to his corps for him to be able to follow the activities of that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, may we have called up P1328, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is an order. It says, Joint Command dated the 15th of April 1999, 455-148 is the number. General, this registration number, to what unit of the Yugoslav Army does it belong? Which unit uses that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 455, that's the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we'll come to look at the document in its entirety but it says here that it is map 1:50.000. Now, can this document be used without a map?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you must have a map, the specific map written there for the document to be complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you please focus on point 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lower down in the English or the following page in the English version, please. Next page. Item 2 next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The title there is "Joint Command." Now, as a layman, I'd like to know the following: Here we have a task of the Pristina Corps as it says in item 2; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And then it says in paragraph 2, the task "Support the MUP forces in the blockade." Now, if it's a Joint Command, do all the units which are being deployed, do they all belong to that Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so, but I don't really understand your question and how you refer to the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: As a layman, if it says Pristina Corps assignment or task it says, support MUP forces, and we have a command that is in charge of all the units, so both the police and the army units, would this kind of formulation be used, or would it be the task and assignment of all the units?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I understand your question now. It would be the task of all the units, and that's what it should specify. It should specifically say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday you commented on item 5, the tasks of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we go to the next page in the English version and in the Serbian, please, so next page, please, point 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: To which unit was this task issued in this order?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose there was something that went before, but without a doubt here it says that the task is issued to the 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the next page in the Serbian version, please, so you can see the whole of point 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here the task was issued to only this brigade and nobody else, that's quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, according to this, could any other unit act upon this order except the 125th Motorised Brigade regardless of whether it was a military one or a MUP unit?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you something else. Do you remember the first item of point 2 of this order, or rather, paragraph, and it says Pristina Corps supports the MUP for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat that reference, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In point 5 where it says "tasks," is there any task or assignment for an armed non-Siptar population to undertake?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll have to repeat my question, I see. It was point 2, and there we see that the Pristina Corps regarding the non-Siptar organisation in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot follow the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, bearing in mind point 5, was there any task for an armed non-Siptar population?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said no, I considered that there wasn't a task for anybody else except for the 125th Brigade, so there was no task as far as this population was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the orders, what would item 2 contain in an order generally?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2 in an order is in fact an item from the order of the Supreme Command written out again, copied out, so the Pristina Corps could have received this kind of order and task only from the 3rd Army or it could formulate its own tasks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now may we turn to the last page -- last page of the document I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is there a signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there's no signature, and it doesn't say who the commander is and it doesn't say who wrote it, who typed it up. Yesterday I said several times what my opinion was of unsigned documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to have D104, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, what we have before us is an order, to rout and destroy the STS in the area of Malo Kosovo on the 22nd of March, 1999, and it says in the heading, Joint Command for KiM, Kosovo and Metohija Strictly Confidential Number 455-56. This registration number, what unit does it belong to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the last page of this document. And also if you could just note or remember the number of this order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't got a pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We are just going to use the last number. Could we please have the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Has this order been signed?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there's no signature, and it doesn't say who the commander of this Joint Command is, and it doesn't say who actually wrote this up. And also, no command can exist without a military commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, sir, according to the rules, who can amend this kind of order? I mean, once an order is adopted, who is authorised to amend it?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any order including this one can only be amended by the person who passed the order in the first place, who issued the order and who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask for document D105, please. Could we please zoom in on the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, can you give us the number of this document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strictly Confidential Number 455-56/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: "/1," do you remember the number of the order a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What does "/1" mean?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That this is a continuation of that document, or rather, that this number is in the same place in the log-book and that both documents have to be archived one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the date on this document is?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd -- now, I cannot see this very well, I cannot see the month very well. 1999. It looks like a 5 but, I'm sorry, I'm not sure. No, no, the 22nd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see the title of the document, as it were?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is "Amendment to the decision on supporting the MUP forces in breaking up and destroying the STS in the area of Malo Kosovo" and underneath it says which maps should be used when this amendment is being carried through.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have the last page of the document, if possible. That's right, yes, that's what we wanted to have enlarged, where the signature is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, can you see whether this amendment has a signature and a stamp?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a clear signature here and a stamp. This is a legal document and the only right kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that it's the signature of the commander of the Pristina Corps, Major-General Vladimir Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recognise his signature?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, in view of this document and in view of the previous document, this is 455-56/1 and the other one is 455-56, who -- I mean, well, if we have this amendment here, what does that tell us?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that can tell us the situation had changed, that there was an indispensable need to make certain corrections in the decision so that it could be properly carried through and the commander of the Pristina Corps decided to write up an amendment on the basis of which certain combat activities will possibly be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And who is authorised to amend the basic document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander, General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to ask if we could get document D0 -- rather, P1523, please. Page 3 in Serbian, page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So this is the briefing of the 18th of April, 1999. The Chief of the General Staff of the Supreme Command is making the concluding remarks and he says one should look into when the telegram was sent to the 3rd Army command, "ask when the telegram was delivered," and you said or rather, you wanted to say a bit more, you wanted to give us a wider explanation.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask you kindly if I could have a look at it here, I would like to read this. I would like to read the actual wording. I didn't quite catch it. I mean, the page is here but could we just have a lowered, scrolled up or scrolled down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Number 6?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, now we have it. Can I see the next page in the Serbian version?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, yes. Yes, yes, the next page. "Ask when the telegram was delivered."

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I do remember that at the evening meeting concerning an analysis of the situation on the front line, we were analysing the situation, the Chief of General Staff gave me the task of checking when the telegram arrived, when it was delivered, and when it was acted upon. Actually, the chief of the staff of the Supreme Command was in a hurry to send this telegram hoping that it would yield fruit. However, the telegram was not delivered properly and on time probably because perhaps that night there had been some heavy bombing and the army commander could not move about freely and a courier couldn't either. We have precise information on the telegram as to when it was sent --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'd like to ask if we could have on our screens P1236, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's tab 27 in your binder but you will see it on the screen as well. You see?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did deal with this, and we have here a report of the commander of the 3rd Army sent to the Chief of General Staff when the telegram was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, I asked you to have a look at tab 26. You started talking about the sending of the telegram.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that the question relates to the bottom of this telegram, when it was sent from the Supreme Command staff. On every telegram we have a stamp, a signature, and a date like here, the 17th of April, 1999, and also the hour and minute along with the signature as to when it was brought for coding and then when it was registered and it was sent, so it was sent at 2000 hours, 40 minutes. And then it was fully handed over at 2155, that is to say there was confirmation received from Pristina or wherever that it was properly received with no error.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notify the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command about what you found out?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And now could you look at tab 27, that's the next document, or rather P1449.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is a report of the command of the 3rd Army dated the 20th of April, 1999. General, on the last page could you have a look at the square stamp, and could you you interpret it for us?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is proof of the fact that this telegram was received at the coding department by -- at a certain moment when it was sent on the 20th of April, 1999. At 1205, that's when it was processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And underneath that, underneath the stamp, who wrote that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The part that is typed in Cyrillic where it says "submitted to" that was done by someone at the Supreme Command staff who received this telegram and he wrote who it was sent to. Since there are several addressees where information was sought, he decided probably to send copies to assistant Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command for operations and staff affairs, and the chief of the operations administration, that is to me, and to the chief of KoV administration, because it wasn't only one person who was in charge of everything that was contained in this telegram. At the end is the signature of the person who certifies that this document is authentic, or rather that the photocopy of this document is authentic, and he signed here, it's Colonel Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General, for having come to testify in our case. Thank you, Your Honours. I have completed my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have our break now and resume at 11.00. There are some questions of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Judge Baird will ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, General, you've been giving evidence for some time so I shall try to be as brief as possible. There are one or two very small points about which I should like some clarification, and I'm confident that you can assist me in that area. What I shall do, I shall give you an idea of the evidence so that I can put the question in perspective. Now, I'm referring to Exhibit P888, and this is the report from the 3rd Army forward command post dated 25th May, 1999 addressed to the Supreme Command staff, Chief of Staff, in person. It is classified as military secret, strictly confidential. Do you recollect this?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recollect this document from the courtroom and also from the proofing session during my last testimony here, but I don't remember it from the actual time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: All right. But you stated that during the war you had not seen that document?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that I hadn't seen the document and that it did not arrive at the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: And Mr. Djurdjic asked you to describe the procedure of receipt when a document such as that one was sent to the Chief of the Supreme Command in person, and you gave a brief description of the procedure. You said that if a document like that were sent to the Chief of Staff, then the office of the chief receives it when it is still sealed, the Chef de Cabinet receives it, puts a stamp at the bottom, as to who received it, where it was sent, later on et cetera. Now, my question to you, General, is this: Would there ever have been instances when the particular document was so very personal and confidential that the Chef de Cabinet would not open it at all but would pass it unopened to the Chief of the Supreme Staff who in turn would open it, read it, and if he so desires he then passes it back to the Chef de Cabinet; would that be possible at all?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle you don't open an envelope of that kind in the office. It comes sealed to the Chief of the Supreme Command staff, having passed through anti-diversionary or sabotage control and then the Chef de Cabinet opens it with scissors, takes it out, and hands it over to the Chief of the Supreme Command staff. Only afterwards is the procedure put in place whereby a stamp it placed on it, registration, so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So there's never a situation where the letter goes to the Chief of Staff without being opened by the Chef de Cabinet?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know whether it ever happened or not. I can't say that it actually didn't, but I don't know of any such thing happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Now, on that very situation, you were asked to describe the procedure when a document of that kind was sent to the Chief of the General Staff, and you said that when the report like that arrived or was handed to him, he would review it and he would invite his closest associates to review it, and at the evening briefing on combat readiness, you all would study it and voice your opinions and proposals. Do you recollect this?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until the evening briefing we were supposed to examine it and then put forward proposals at the evening briefing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Would the Chief of Supreme Command be absolutely bound to invite his associates to review the document and to have it discussed at the evening briefings? I mean, was he absolutely bound by this procedure, or could he have said to the Chef de Cabinet, Look here, I don't want all my associates to see this, I just want two or three; could that have happened?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's possible, but the style of work, the way in which the Chief of the Supreme Command staff General Ojdanic, whom I've known for over 40 years, worked and how he functioned, everybody who was connected with this document must be informed so that he could hear as many different opinions and proposals as possible to be able to make the right decision or issue the right order having heard all that. So he always advocated team-work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I see. Now, tell me, General, was it ever brought to your attention as chief of the first operation administration at the General Staff, that during the war there were frequent altercations at the check-points manned by the MUP and the military police units springing from the fact that the MUP members permitted criminal acts by their fellow MUP members and civilians such as appropriation of motor vehicles, and technical goods and so on, ever at all?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that anything like that happened. I was never informed about anything like that happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I see. Now, Ms. Petersen - and this is my last question - Ms. Petersen asked you about Combat Report Number 28 from the Supreme Command staff. It's dated 21st April, 1999, and she referred to section 2.4, the second paragraph, where it was stated, I would summarise her, I would summarise here, that between 19 and 20 April 1999, about 3.000 people crossed from KiM to Macedonia escorted by the MUP. She then asked if we conclude from the report that the MUP were walking alongside the column, and you gave your answer and you ended the answer saying that she was right, it was written there and "we did not hide it that this column passed through there and went towards Macedonia, and it says clearly escorted by the MUP." And then there was a follow-up question and you answered that "it did say that the 3.000 people crossed from Kosovo to Macedonia." Now, do you recollect this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recollect it, but I'm not quite sure that I used all those words since they had crossed from Kosovo to the rest of Serbia and then across the village of Miratovac, went towards the border which is something else, and I'm even not sure whether that column ever left Serbia to go to Macedonia but that it was stopped at the border and sent back, and we have that in some of the later reports, but yes, I do remember that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Now, are you in a position, General, to say why the MUP escorted these 3.000 people?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume -- I hope you'll understand me, all I can do is to assume why, assume the reason. There might have been a number of reasons. One of the reasons was to prevent somebody in the forest, along the road at night, that they should not be fired at by some forces and that that be ascribed to the MUP or the army. And that the Serbs in retaliation on Serbs in retaliation for certain ill-deeds committed in their own villages perhaps might have ambushed them and massacred them or to prevent them from entering a minefield along the border belt and be killed that way so these are all possible reasons that I can see. Or they might have been asked by some of the locals to escort them in safety and security and to ensure that they have no problems in crossing the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Protection?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE CURCIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know that that completes the questions. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance, for the assistance you've been able to give, and you may now return to your normal activities. A Court Officer will show you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I am offering to basically do the same thing that Mr. Stamp did the other day if it would assist the Court. We have a comparison of exhibit numbers that were used with this witness in the Milutinovic case and corresponding numbers that have come in that were tendered in this case, if that would assist the Court. I know that we're working on a more permanent solution to this -- trying to correspond the numbers, but if it would assist, in the meantime I could give the ones right now or we could just wait until we have a more permanent solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for your offer, but we think it would be just complicating life to have such details after every witness and it would be better to wait for a co-ordinated overall comparison. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, is it you that I look to? Every time I turn around I see a different lineup in the team there.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honours. It's the youth that are in the front lines today, so we are going to deal with the next witness in my person, and the next Defence witness is Mr. Rade Cucak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will it be Ms. Kravetz or Mr. Behar? Mr. Behar, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read the affirmation that is shown to you now on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Popovic has questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cucak.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Cucak, before we begin the examination-in-chief, I'd like to ask you to speak slowly, and since you and I speak the same language, could you make a pause between my question and your answer, and that will facilitate the work of the interpreters and they will be able to do their job properly. Could you start off by giving us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: My name is Rade Cucak.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I was born on the 28th of November 1947 in a small village along the banks of the Una River 25 kilometres away from Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Cucak, on the 17th of August, 2007, did you give a statement to the Ojdanic Defence team, and did you sign that statement personally?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: On that day I did give a statement, and I personally signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to approach the microphones, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before this Court -- Mr. Cucak, I'm going to ask you for the benefit of the interpreters so that they can hear everything you say, could you approach the microphone, please. Get a little closer to the microphones. Yes, thank you. And I'll repeat my last question. Have you testified before this Tribunal in the Milutinovic et al trial on the 31st of August and the 4th of September, 2007?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And during the proofing session for today's testimony, did you have an opportunity of reading through your testimony given in the Milutinovic trial?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And would you give the same answers to all the questions posed to you and recorded in the transcript, would you give the same answers today as you did then if you were to be asked those questions?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I would give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, may I ask you to pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I would like to tender Mr. Cucak's statement of the 17th of August, 2007, which is Exhibit 006-0883.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you gave your statement in August of 2007, when you prepared it and signed it, are the answers that you gave then the answers that you would -- or the evidence that you gave in that statement what you would say today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, mostly I would say the same today. I didn't look at the details of the statement again. I looked through it, of course. It was a long time ago when I gave the statement and signed it, but, yes, I would mostly, I suppose, give the same answers that I did then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statement will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00569. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The transcript will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00570. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am now going to read out a summary of the witness statement. In his testimony, the witness will speak about the organisation and methods of the application of the system for marking the state borders of the FRY towards neighbouring countries and the realisation of international agreements linked to border questions for the period from 1987 to 2003. The witness was appointed to hold various posts in the JNA and Yugoslav Army until 2003 when he retired with the rank of colonel. From 1987 onwards, he was the chief of the department within the frameworks of the first administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia which dealt with border questions. While he occupied functions closely linked to matters of the state border, the witness was a member of many state and international commissions and other bodies dealing with the establishment and adoption of international rules and regulations linked to borders. The witness will explain to us what a border regime means, a border incident means, violation of border incidents, border belt, and the establishment and delineation of the border belt. He will explain what actions and procedure were undertaken within the border belt in order to protects the borders of the FRY and protect the territorial integrity and sovereignty of the FRY. He will also explain that it was the basic task of each army, including the Army of Yugoslavia, and is its task to secure the borders of its country in peacetime. The witness will quote legal acts and documents regulating the issues that we are discussing, and he will go on to explain that the situation along the state border was constantly monitored by the department for state borders which was a component part of the operative department of the sector for operative staff affairs of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. The witness will provide essential data linked to the border with the Republic of Albania. He will confirm that from the first half of 1995 members of the VJ dealing with border issues started to observe and notice increasing numbers of armed civilians on the territory of the Republic of Albania right along the border, or rather that during this same period of time, the number of border incidents began to increase, which culminated with the killing and wounding of Yugoslav border officials. He will also speak about the joint commissions of Yugoslavia and Albania, established to deal with border incidents, however, because the Albania state organs refuse to co-operate, such commissions completely lost all importance. The witness will also speak about border incidents which took place during 1998 and 1999 and which were a direct consequence of the activities of the KLA. The witness will confirm to us how many members of the Army of Yugoslavia lost their lives and how many members of the border units who were securing the border towards Albania and how many were wounded during terrorist attacks. He will confirm that the protection of lives of the members of the VJ who were carrying out their duties along the border with Albania and Macedonia was the only reason for the re-establishment of the border belt. After the border belt was established in accordance with the situation on the ground, it made it possible for members of the VJ to apply different tactics of securing the state border in an effort to preserve the sovereignty of the FRY. The witness will confirm that the units that were securing the border did not get any special instructions related to refugees.
