They were careful when there were attempts to cross the border illegally, and if such persons were captured, they were handed over to appropriate institutions. The witness is going to speak of what happened during NATO bombing and joint activities of NATO and the KLA along the border of the FRY and the Republic of Albania. He is going to speak about a document that was issued by the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs which registers all the incidents that occurred on the border of the FRY during 1998 and 1999 and that are a result of the activities of terrorists along the border with the Republic of Albania. The witness is also going to speak to us about the way in which reports were compiled when the state of war was proclaimed and the information that he received on the situation along the border. That would be a summary of this witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cucak, were you a member of the Army of Yugoslavia, and if so until when?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Army of Yugoslavia from the date when I entered the military academy. That was a long time ago in 1966. And I was a member all the way up until 2003 when I was pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, what rank did you hold at the moment when you were pensioned off?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I was a colonel at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to us briefly which positions you held within the Army of Yugoslavia during the course of your military career?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: During my military career I started with the lowest ranking positions such as platoon commander and company commander, then I was an officer in the escort of the supreme commander of the Army of Yugoslavia Josip Broz Tito, then Comrade Josip Broz Tito. Then I worked as an operations officer in the organ for operations in training, then I was battalion commander, then the brigade commander. I also did different types of work in border affairs, starting off as desk officer and I ended up as a chief of that service in the VJ and the last few years I spent as head of the state border service in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and I dealt with different questions related to international treaties and other border related matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the state border is going to be the main topic of your testimony today, tell us first and foremost what are the laws that regulate the state border?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I will be able to say what the basic law in this field is and that is the law on crossing the state border and movement within the border belt. There are other bylaws that regulate details on the basis of the aforementioned law.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will probably be speaking a bit outside the period of 1998 and 1999 as well, but could you tell us what your duties were in the VJ in 1998 and 1999? I'm primarily referring to the situation when a state of war was declared during the aggression of NATO against the FRY.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: At that time I was head of the department for the border in the first administration of the General Staff. That was a department that dealt with organising the functioning of the system of the state border. That is to say, the organisation and functioning of securing the state border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That is to say, the overall border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Of course, including that particular part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia border.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on to a more detailed analysis of the situation along the border, can you explain to us as laypeople what the border regime means, also what does the border belt mean and what is a border incident?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: First of all, although that was not a question that was put to me, can I first say what the border actually is? The border is a line that cuts across the territory of a country. Also it includes the air above it and the land below it. It separates the territory of one sovereign country from another. As for the border belt, the border belt is part of the territory or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in relation to that border-line that goes in-depth in the territory and that is a belt within which the security organs exercise the rights vested in them by the law and that means exercising control over the situation at the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The border regime?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The border regime. That is a set of legal and other regulations setting the rights of citizens in the border belt in relation to border units and make it possible for them to function in the system of securing the state border within the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about a border incident?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, a border incident, that is any violation of the state order which excludes an infringement upon the territorial integrity and sovereignty of a state. That is to say that borders incidents are actions that take place at the border but without infringing upon the sovereignty of the state concerned, that is what a border incident is. Or rather, bringing into question - perhaps that would be a better way of putting it - of the sovereignty of the other state involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. A special part of your testimony is going to pertain to the border belt. You told us what the border belt is, and could you also tell us now according to law how big is the border belt and how is it defined?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, you see, the law on crossing the state border and moving within the border belt stipulates that the border belt runs along the state border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia 100 metres from that particular line. And if necessary, it can go even further in-depth, so basically it is 100 metres but it can be even bigger. So that is the belt that makes it possible for the organs in charge to exercise their duty along the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, when you say 100 metres, does that mean that at each and every point at the border that is 100 metres from the border there is a marking of the border belt, and how is it marked? In metres or how do you do it?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The border belt is not marked in terms of metres. There are sign posts at roads in the area that say, Attention, border belt. So persons entering the border belt have to have the right kind of documents for entering the border belt. Now, the border belt is only marked on different landmarks and that's how it's defined. So it's not only 100 metres away from the border, no. It depends on the terrain itself. So whoever gets that decision that has to do with the state border and that is published in the Official Gazette of the state, everyone can see where this border belt actually is.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, however, I'd like to check whether I'm actually understanding what you are saying. If the state border is marked with particular objects on the ground, does that mean that in certain places the border belt can be narrower or wider than those 100 metres, or is 100 metres the rule that has to be observed?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I said that according to law, it was 100 metres in the case of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in relation to the state border, but it also run further in-depth in relation to the state border, only when it would so be proposed by the appropriate state organ or institution. Rather, it would be proposed by a different organ, but then the government would have to pass a decision to that effect, that the border belt is bigger than 100 metres from the state border. So it is only the government that could pass that kind of decision ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the powers of the members of the Army of Yugoslavia, tell me, what authority did they have in the border belt, and what authority did they have outside the border belt?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, you see, the members of the Army of Yugoslavia secure the border in the border belt, that is to say, they served within the border belt outside built-up areas, and also apart from border crossings. This -- these other parts that I referred to just now were under the MUP or rather, other organs that exercised their duties in the area. For example, the customs office. And outside built-up areas and apart from actual border crossings it was the Army of Yugoslavia that exercised its duties. They had the right to stop persons, take their IDs, and even bring them into custody if they did not have appropriate weapons and they could even use fire-arms if it had to do with armed individuals or armed groups that were putting point up resistance. If they were chasing persons in the border area, they had the right to pursue these persons until this activity would be taken over by the Ministry of the Interior. Outside the border belt, the members of the VJ only had the right to intervene if they came across an armed group that fired at them, but not in other cases. They didn't have the right to respond in that way either.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll deal with border belt a bit more when we go through the documentation that I'm going to show you. However, in order to move on, could you tell me briefly what the situation was like between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Albania in the beginning of 1998 and during 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, the border towards the Republic of Albania was not only burdened -- or rather, it became burdened as it were in 1998 when there was a coup or a revolution in the territory of the Republic of Albania, I don't know what it was called then, that is when all border facilities on the Albanian sides were held by persons unknown. We could see from our border, observers did see this that unknown individuals were taking position of weapons and facilities on the Albanian side, and after that a large number of persons appeared on the border with Yugoslavia but they were moving in the border belt on the Albanian side. Also when our border officials would see armed persons moving about in civilian clothes but with heavy weapons when you see that they did not have say hunting guns or something like that, this was something that was experienced as a burden as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak slower.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I will do my best. I get carried away.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what problems did you have mostly linked to the border with the Republic of Albania, and what were the border incidents which happened mostly? What type of incident?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, allow me, first of all -- well, to answer the question of what these border incidents were, I have to say, first of all, that the border existed, or rather, the border became burdened with this vast quantity of weapons, and at the time a large number of individuals attempted to cross the border illegally, and go to Albania, either individually or in smaller groups. Next there were some individuals, and this was established, had the necessary papers to cross into Albania legally, and then with weapons and military equipment, they attempted to come back across the state border illegally and come back to the territory of the FRY. And next there were registered a large number of cases, I don't know the exact number now, but anyway, many cases where individuals loaded up horses with weapons and military equipment belonging to the FRY, they were caught that way, and some people loaded up some animals and set them free on the territory of Yugoslavia, and usually animals and horses go back to the home they have come from. So the border was being closed down and then there were terrorist actions coming from Albanian territory more and more with this restriction of border crossing, and they used various weapons, mortars, and so on, machine-guns, anti-aircraft cannons, and so on directly from Albanian territory, so the FRY came under threat from Albanian territory and on the other hand, there was open aggression with assistance from Albania's allies and so on, so those were mostly the kind of incidents that took place in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when we speak of the expansion of the border belt, and I'm referring to 1998, tell us, please, when was the border belt first expanded?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, when at the beginning of 1998 border incidents started happening and when they had serious consequences and needed fire support, the General Staff border service that I headed proposed to the officers in the General Staff and the Chief of the General Staff and the chief of the first administration and through him the Chief of the General Staff of course, that given the situation and given the fact that there were firing incidents along the border belt, that the need arose for expanding the border belt, so that the organs that were positioned along the border with the 100-metre depth should withdraw and prevent themselves from being targets for these groups. So at the time there were mountains in the Pastrik area in general, that in that section, the border belt should be expanded somewhat. The General Staff gave its permission and we prepared a decision put through the Ministry of Defence and put to the government, and the decision was taken, don't hold me it to the exact date, but I think that it came into force in April or mid-April, I'm not sure of the exact date. If I had the decision in front of me, I could see what the exact date of that was. In 1998 of course. I'm referring to 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me ask you this: Was it acted upon, as you have described to us thus far, did they pin-point points along the border belt?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, the border belt was defined on the ground straightaway and even minor roads and paths that entered the border belt would -- there would be a notice warning citizens that they were entering a border belt. And the citizens were informed of the decision taken by the information media and a proclamation stating that a border belt was in existence. And the citizens already knew what their rights and duties were with respect to movement around the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have Defence Exhibit D006-1273 called up, please. Thank you. And with the Trial Chamber's permission, could the witness be handed the binder with the documents that we shall be dealing with during this session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you will find the document under number 1, and it is dated the 17th of April, 1998. It is the Pristina Corps Command to the security administration of the Army of Yugoslavia, the security department, and it reads as follows: "On the 16th of April, 1998, at 0145 hours, a group of terrorists (an estimated 50 to 60 men) in the Morina border post sector, near C-7, crossed from the territory of the Republic of Albania into the territory of the FRY with 12 horses loaded up with weapons and military equipment. A state border security organ opened fire, dispersing the group of terrorists. The terrorists returned fire during the pullout and at the same time fire was opened on our state border security organ from the territory of the Republic of Albania." First of all, may we have your comments. Is that an example of the sort of incidents that took place along the border belt in 1998, that is to say between -- the border between Albania and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: This is unfortunately only one such incident that took place along the state border with -- the border with the Republic of Albania facing Kosovo and Metohija. There were many more such incidents which were far more serious than this particular one, and of course, there were some minor incidents as well, but we are dealing with the beginning of 1998 or rather the first half of 1998 when there were extensive border incidents along the borders between Albania and Yugoslavia threatening Yugoslavia's security and integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we see the date there as being the 17th of April. You said that the first time the border belt was extended was when?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Sometime during April. It came in to force in mid-April, so this extension of the border belt -- well, this is an indicator telling us that we had to extend the border belt, had to take that measure for the army to be able to exercise its right under the law to protect and safe-guard the countries territory and integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's just be very precise. This extension of the border belt from April 1998, what part of the border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did it refer to?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The April border belt expansion related to the entire stretch of the border with Albania, from the Bojana River estuary into the sea with a point that was not precisely established at the time but anyway was bordering on the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you focus on the last sentence in that paragraph where it says: "The superior command was immediately informed. A report was sent to LMK-4 local mixed commission, and requests were made for announcement of a border incident, a meeting with LMK-4 and joint on-site investigation." What does this LMK-4 mean in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, let me explain. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia vis-à-vis neighbouring countries had signed an international agreement on state borders, that's what it was called, and it regulated many issues, many questions related to the border. So it was on the basis of this international agreement that mixed commissions were set up at the level of states to deal with violations of the border regime and border incidents as a more severe form of that. And also other questions linked to the state border. Now, in addition to this main mixed commission, or let me say that the main mixed commission did not come under the authority of the state -- state organs appointed by the government, but in addition to these mixed commissions, there were local commissions too and they covered part of the territory, or rather, adapted to individual sectors and entrances to Albania. So along the border with Albania there were five sector commissions, one of which was along the coast dealing with questions of the sea. The third was in Potkovica, the fourth was in Djakovica and Prizren. And every local commission, the leaders and officials of which were from the Ministry of the Interior and from the border units that provided security for that belt usually there was a commander of the border battalion, and their task was when any untoward event occurred along the border with Albania, that they should issue a warning to the Albanian side and ask them to make an on-site investigation and established facts to try and establish what had happened, what kind of border incident had taken place. And if not, then they could leave the task to the international mixed commission to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, now, for the transcript, the main mixed commission, where did that come, under whose authority was that?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The main mixed commission was under the state organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's what you said but it was wrongly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, now let's turn to page 2 in both versions, the Serbian and the English, or rather the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It says their members of the 53rd Border Battalion did not return fire but warned LMK-4 that fire had been opened on members of the VJ from the the Albanian side and asked that the chairman of the Albanian LMK-4 side Mr. Selim Demusi go to the territory of Albania and prevent fire from being opened on members of the VJ from the territory of Albania. Having contacted the attackers Selim Demusi said that he could not control them because they were a gang and asked that the LMK-4 return without completing their mission because as a member of the Albanian LMK-4 side, he could not guarantee the safety of VJ members and the Yugoslav LMK-4 side. May we have a brief comment to what I've just read out?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: This is a case I'm particularly familiar with. It was one of the rare times when the Albanian side agreed to go out with a local commission to carry out an on-site investigation of the territory where the border incident had occurred. This was a very rare occasion. They went on site while both sides did. The Joint Commission made up of representatives of both sides, and at that point the organs providing security for the state borders provided security on that occasion. So as to secure the people and ensure their safety, the people conducting the on-site investigation from -- at that point they were opened fire on from the Albanian side, and our member of the mixed commission intervened and asked the Albanian representative to calm the situation down, and he did indeed go to the territory of Albania where this had happened. He came back sometime later and said what he said, that they were terrorists bands or gangs or whatever, moving around the border belt area. So that is the substance of this particular incident, and I could add some things, perhaps I could do so now.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: How would you assess the co-operation between the state organs and organs in general who were supposed to take part on the Albanian side in these Joint Commissions dealing with these issues?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, here is my assessment. I'd like to make an observation and that will indicate to you what kind of co-operation that was. Well, the Albanian side, the mixed commission sat every year, met every year, once on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the next time on Albanian territory. The last such session that was held of this mixed commission, took place on the territory of the FRY. And that was in 1996. I think it was held in Potkovica, and ever since that meeting was held, there were no other meetings because the Albanian side was supposed to host the following meeting and they did not wish do so. They did not wish to implement the agreement that we had whereby annual meeting would be held. They did not schedule any such meeting and the initiative taken from -- by the General Staff through the foreign ministry to offer the Albanian side, or rather, for the FRY to host a new meeting to resolve the incidents, there was that kind of proposal because the incidents had become more and more prevalent. Minor ones and more serious ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as Exhibit D00571. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have D006-1358, a Defence document to be called up next, please. It is document number 2 in your set, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: As we can see, we have the 53rd Border Battalion command and an assessment of endangered areas and, or rather, axes and the estimate of forces required for full heightened security, and in point 1 it lists the most endangered axes from 1 to 11. I won't go into that in detail, but anyway, on the last page which is page D006-1360 in the B/C/S version and D006-1363 for the English. It says in the last sentence there: "At present for providing security along the line we have 540 soldiers and 68 officers which means that we're lacking 960 soldiers and 62 officers." Now, linked to what I have just read out, the most threatened axes and the number of officers and soldiers needed and lacking along those axes.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Could I please go back a bit, particularly in relation to this document. When it became obvious that after the first -- the border belt was extended for the first time, the situation became even more serious. As soon as -- there were a large number of incidents that were actually discovered. So the professional service of the Army of Yugoslavia asked for an assessment to be made of threats to the border belt. I see here that it was the Pristina Corps that asked the 53rd Border Battalion to carry this out. They were located in Djakovica. They were asked to see where the threats were along which axis. And it was the 57th in Urosevac that also received such orders. They were supposed to see which axes and which roads were threatened and the question was whether we really had sufficient forces to deal with the situation. It wasn't only lighter violation, but very serious violations that were at hand, seriously violating the territorial integrity and sovereignty of the country. On the basis is of these documents, thought was given how to prevent these terrorist incursions from the territory of the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to have this document admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be admitted as Exhibit Number D00572. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to what you said when you finished answering the last question, could we please have document D320 on our screens now. It's number 3 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's a letter. A piece of information of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia dated the 16th of July, 1998. He is sending it to the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs Mr. General Jovanovic who was federal minister at the time. And it says here, "In order to launch a diplomatic initiative in international organizations and institutions, the OSCE and the United Nations in particular, we are hereby forwarding to you a report on the involvement of the Republic of Albania in events in Kosovo and Metohija, a list of border incidents that occurred on the border with the Republic of Albania between the 1st of January 1998 and --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The poor lady interpreting needed to catch a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to the interpreters. We are trying to catch up in terms of time because we seem to be lagging behind this week, but of course we don't want to do it at the expense of the interpreters, so I will slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I point out that we do have the document, you do not need to read large parts of it aloud. That could save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take that into account, Your Honour. This is where the part that I wanted to read out actually ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you heard what I read out to you, and could we please have a brief comment from you?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: This was a regular thing that the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia or rather, the first administration and the department -- the border department inform the appropriate organs about the situation at the state border, not only in Kosovo, but in relation to all states that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had a border with. However, this indicates a serious violation that borders on aggression, if you will, in view of their characteristics. All of these were armed provocations or attempted incursions by armed groups bringing in large quantities of military equipment as well. This was rightly interpreted as a type of aggression against the state without a declaration of war. I looked at this survey, I happened to see it now -- I saw it a long time ago but --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we'll get to that, but let's do things in the right order.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to have page 5 called up, please, in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You see this is a survey of border incidents along the border with the Republic of Albania between the 1st of January, 1998 and the 30th of June, 1998. I don't want to dwell on it any longer, but I did notice something. If one were to analyse this survey you would see that up until mid-April there were 14 violations from the 1st of January until the 15th of April and from the 15th of April until the 30th of June, so it's the same period of time, there were 46 incidents. Can you give us your comment on this? You spoke about the extension of the border belt. Does that have anything do with that, and if so, what is it exactly?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, when we extended -- no, not extended, that would not be the right term to use. It is people who are not very knowledgeable about borders that use that term. It was actually establishing the border belt that went beyond 100 metres. And it's the federal government that decides on that. When we were to establish the border belt we had to deal with these different violations coming from the Republic of Albania. When we went further in-depth in term of our own territory, then more organs could be engaged in the area of their activity. They could deal with inaccessible areas, areas that are not accessible even on horseback, only on foot. Then there was an increase in captured -- in the number of captured individuals carrying equipment, et cetera, on the border. When groups were discovered in that area, then this -- that had a reflection on the number of groups coming from the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 13 in B/C/S please now. I don't think that this page does not exist in the English version. We did send it to the translation service to have that page translated and the next one. I'm going to deal with this page very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is a list of weapons that were seized. What we see on our screens now is page 9, and I had asked for page 13. Or rather, it's the next page, the one after this one, the one after this one is the one that I'm talking about. So that is a list of seized weapons and other military equipment on the border with the Republic of Albania between the 1st of January and the 8th of June, 1998. Colonel, very briefly, a comment on this table. I would be interested in more -- I would be interested in heavy weaponry, we see that there are small arms here as well.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Let me say straightaway that you don't have to be a military expert to draw the right conclusion on the basis of this list of seized weapons. You can see that the quantity of weapons recorded here is sufficient to arm two battalion strength units at least. So this is military equipment and weaponry for combat activities. It is obvious that this is intended to arm units that are supposed to engage in combat, if you look at everything that is listed here, so these are stronger manoeuvring forces for activity in the area of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Four -- three recoilless guns, right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 16, or rather, 16 mortars.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, 16 mortars. So these would be sufficient for two battalions. Only in terms of mortars, and look at how many hand-held rocket-launchers, 927, that's the number here. It shows that the intention of those who carry these weapons was the establishment of groups for destroying facilities not only in the border belt but probably throughout the territory of Kosovo and perhaps even beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. Thank you. Now I'm going to like to ask for D006-1261.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Parker, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, D320 was the document we saw previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, the Official Gazette of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia dated the 21st of July, 1998, and the decision of establishing the border belt adjacent to sections of the state border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So this is what you've been insisting upon, establishing the border belt, not extending it?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the basis of this decision, for which sections was the border belt established, how was it done? Could you please answer that first and then we'll look into the reasons.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The decision on establishing the border belt or rather this decision pertains to the state border towards the Republic of Albania. Let me put it this way, from the mouth of the Bojana River up to the tri-lateral border with the Republic of Albania -- of -- that hadn't been regulated yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the Republic of Macedonia, that's what it also says, so does it pertain towards -- to the border towards the Republic of Macedonia as well? Number 2 on the right.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: On that a same page that you are looking at, on the right-hand side, it says the border belt is being extended and then it says --

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, but it's the first part that I've been speaking of. I thought you asked me about that. If you are referring to the entire area, so it is from the mouth of the Bojana River to the tri-lateral border with Macedonia that hadn't been established yet, and then Macedonia from the tri-lateral border with Albania all the way to the border with Bulgaria.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to what you said to us about April, that was the establishment of the border belt facing the Republic of Albania, now we are talking about establishing the border belt facing the Republic of Macedonia. What is the reason for that decision?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I'll tell you. Again I have to go back a bit. When the border belt was extended the previous time, the deployment of forces on the border belt for securing the state border was far more favourable and more concealed so they could apply different tactics in the system of securing the state border which made it possible for them to capture many illegal border crossers and to capture large quantities of equipment. It also made it possible for us to further strengthen the forces engaged in securing the state border precisely because it was realised that this was a major threat. If I can call them that, these terrorists forces from the Republic of Albania realised that that was the case and then they changed their methodology. Equipment was taken from Albania to Macedonia and then from Macedonia across Mount Sara [phoen] and Gora into the territory of the Federal Republic of Macedonia. That's where we first captured those horses on the Macedonian border with guides. Large quantities were involved. They tried to smuggle in large quantities of equipment, so obviously this involved a change of tactics in order to make it easier for them to bring military equipment from Albania into Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I'd like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number D00573. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: While this document is still on our screens, Colonel, how was the border belt established, in which way?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Like all others it relate -- it was set by a decision regarding the actual situation on the ground, the landmarks on the ground. 400, 500, 700 metres, some were even 1.000. It's not like I read in the media where various individuals said it would only be 500 metres and that would be it. We wanted to cover different roads leading into villages so that people could communicate normally between and among various villages and towns that were their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D168.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this is the first special session of the collegium on the 14th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to have page 18 in B/C/S and page 22 in English. We will deal with this document very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We see what Major-General --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is page 17 in B/C/S and I would like to have page 18, please. Yes, that's the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Major-General Spaso Smiljanic is speaking here and he is saying: "General, sir, on the basis of an order issued by the Chief of the General Staff on the 16th of November, 1998, the 3rd Army Command on the basis of an order of the Chief of General Staff, set up an expert team which inspected the security system and the functioning of the security system on the state border with Albania." My question for you is: What expert team is this? What is it that General Spaso Smiljanic is talking about?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: In order to make things clear to all, I have to go back a bit. After the border was established more in-depth in April, there were masses of individuals who were trying to cross the border illegally that were captured, individuals and groups. When we saw that in that part of the border it was more difficult to get into the territory. There were situations when various forces from the territory from Kosovo and Metohija tried to fire at security organs in the border belt in order to distract their attention from the border, and in that way make it possible for large quantities of weapons to be smuggled in from Albania. Then the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia took measures. They asked for a further strengthening of forces in securing the state border and further improving the system in order to raise its efficiency to a higher level. And that was done, now, I don't remember exactly on which date. I think it was sometime in the beginning of November when this was discussed by the General Staff. Mr. Momcilo Perisic, General Momcilo Perisic who was Chief of General Staff at the time, he took note of that, but he personally went to Kosovo and Metohija to see what the situation was. I don't know who received him down there, and they reported to him and when he returned from there, or rather, it was while he was still down there that he issued an oral commander to -- oral order to the commander of the Pristina Corps to have the entire security system in the border belt analysed. So this expert team was established on the basis of his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have Exhibits D006-1259, Defence document, called up on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you can look at your screen, it will be simpler for you. Anyway, it refers to the organisation of the security system facing the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I don't have it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It will appear in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we zoom into the map which we can now see.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this map, and if so, who compiled it and can you explain to us what the yellow line means and the red dots along it?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I am familiar with this map. This map existed during preparations for additionally expanding the border belt. The yellow colour denotes the existing border belt. Now, the service in the General Staff in charge of borders --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just try and be more precise here, Colonel. The yellow line was the border belt, shows the border belt on the basis of a decision of the 21st of July, 1999, is that it?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, please continue.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Let me just remind you of one point, the security organs were highly efficient but there were quite a lot of victims and attacks carried out along the border in attempts to introduce weapons both through Macedonia and through Albania into the country. So these axes were closed off and additional measures needed to be taken to expand the border belt, or rather, to create the proper conditions for border units to provide security to the country and the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What about the red dots? What do they represent?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, you didn't ask me, I would have answered had you asked me. When my service made a proposal to an organ, it had to submit a detailed proposal substantiated in fact. Now, the red dots here, yes, I can see it now, the red dots are where there was incursion action along the border belt at the various observation posts. And you can see that there was firing from different calibre weapons along these points, along the border belt. That's what these red points show, the firing points, points from which the country was fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's admitted as Exhibit D00574. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must have our next break now, and we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have called up, please, P1343.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And, Witness, it should be document number 8 in your set. It is the minutes from the 8th session, document number 7, minutes of the 8th session, of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 25th of December, 1998, and on page 1 under item 1, we see that the agenda says: "Discussion of the situation on the state border with the Republic of Albania."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page in the Serbian and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, towards the end of that page it says that the border organs of the Army of Yugoslavia in the period from 1st to the 24th of December, 1998, at the Yugoslav Albanian state border, apprehended 676 persons crossing the border illegally.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: What page did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's on the second page, the first page is titled "minutes" where it is in fact the documents of the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council session. There you are, on the next page, fine, that's it. It says that they apprehended 676 persons crossing illegally, about 80 sabotage and terrorists groups were stopped which tried to cross into FRY territory in an organised and violent fashion with quantities of weapons and military equipment, and in the following paragraph it says the Albanian side this year committed 122 border incidents or violations, 99 of which directly infringed upon the sovereignty of the FRY. May we have your comments to that.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: The regular reports were sent to this body for its sessions, and one of the subjects discussed was the situation along the state border and here we wanted to inform the top leadership about the situation along the border. We wanted them to be held -- kept abreast of the situation so that they could take steps to enforce security along the state borders. Now, the number itself indicates that this was a massive influx and many incidents taking place along the state border without counting other incidents that took place elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we take a look at the next document which is Exhibit P1017.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is document number -- well, actually you could look at the screen, and the document will be called up there. This is a report covering two pages mentioned in Major-General Drewienkiewicz's report dated the 23rd of June, 2000. You don't have that document in your binder in actual fact, so please follow it on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may we turn to the next page in B/C/S and in English, please. So the next page. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm going to try briefly to focus your attention on what I'm interested in. Background information is under number 1 and it says, Even if the KLA were instantly disbanded and completely disbanded, the lack of law and order in Albania and the lack of proper Albanian border controls -- have you found it?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I have now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The lack of proper Albanian border controls will force the legal authorities of Kosovo to secure its frontiers. That's the end of that sentence. And another sentence I'd like you to focus on is under item 4 and the subtitle is, Boarder Area, and it says as follows: "There are 32 [Realtime translation read in error "3"] boarder posts or observation towers. The towers are not usually manned as the Albanians use them for target practice. FRY patrols rarely patrol along the actual border as they are shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the transcript, the beginning of the sentence reads, "There are 32 border posts, not three. There are 32 border posts is the beginning of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: May we have your comments?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, this was clear even before that date, it was clear to all of us dealing with the security service at the borders, the observation post after the general chaos in Albania when they stormed the barracks, took away weapons and military equipment, the border observation posts never existed anymore, they existed as features, and they were fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just slow down for the benefit of the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: As I was saying, those facilities, the observation towers ceased to exist not when this was stated, but far before, that is to say in 1997 they were no longer manned, and they had been damaged, the glass, protective glass was shattered, precisely because they were targeted from Albanian territory. Because they were in the best possible area giving very good vantage point to the Serb side of the Albanian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have Exhibit D523 next, please. It should be document number 8 in your set.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, it is titled "Assessment of the Intelligence and Security Situation and Danger to the Security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia," dated February 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]I want us to look at page 18 in the B/C/S, which is page 20 -- it's the document you just turned. Page 18 of the B/C/S and page 24 of the English. Page 24. And can we look at section 5, item 2. So page 24 for the English, please. That's the right English page, but for the B/C/S could we have page 18 and not 14, which is on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, under item 4 it says: "The state border towards Albania and Macedonia continue to reinforce in-depth security along the state border and to the best of your ability prevent the infiltration of weapons and terrorists into Kosovo and Metohija. Consider the possibility of providing appropriate forces to prevent the forced entry of strong terrorist forces and moving the security line deep into the border belt."

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, this was considered and discussed in case there was a peaceful solution that conditions should -- could allow for normal work and life and security of the border belt. And that the border authorities should be further away from the border line because their presence along the border line itself would not be visible. Now, as to the number of border organs, the situation in Kosovo was considered to be unstable for a long period of time and that it was necessary to have rapid intervention forces, not only to cover the border belt, but generally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Colonel. Now, the last few documents that we've looked at talk about different incidents and different ways in which problems occurred and the kinds of problems that existed along the border belt between Albania, Macedonia, and the FRY. Now, what steps were taken to prevent incidents of this kind from happening?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I said something about this previously. The latest incidents that occurred in the area at the time meant that there was firing from a broad area and from Macedonia too on Mount Sara, so that part of the border came under fire and was under threat, and along the whole border belt with Albania. And at that time the General Staff or rather its professional services, once again gave its consideration to these issues and to stepping up efforts to create the necessary conditions for people to be able to live normally in the border belt. So that was their intention, not to suffer losses and to have an efficient service satisfying the security needs of the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we look at D006-1347 the next Defence document, please. D006-1347 is the number. That's right, 1347.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's document number 9 in your set, Colonel. It is dated the 3rd of March, 1999, and it is a report concerning a border incident. Now, without going through the whole document, I'd just like to ask you to focus on what it says tonight at 0015 hours from the territory of the Republic of Albania from the region of their border post at Pogaj a fire was opened targeting -- a fire was opened from artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing has come up on our screens as yet. May I just take a moment to check the number. That's the right document, yes. We see that it goes on to 0045 hours when there was repeated fire from the Albanian side targeting the Gorozup observation post and its crew. So in March 1999, is the situation the same? What was happening along the border?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, in March 1999 there was intensive fire coming in from Albania and here the Yugoslav side tried to inform the Albanian side of the incident through the local mixed commission. However, by this time, the Albanian side did not respond at all. The border still came under fire, and there were a lot of border incidents with serious repercussions, artillery weapons were used to fire at the FRY from Albania, and also terrorist groups infiltrated from Albania or from Kosovo Metohija into the border belt opening fire at the border forces so as to ensure, well, conditionally speaking, free territory for infiltrating manpower and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, what you are saying is this: That terrorist groups could storm the border belt from Kosovo and Metohija but also from Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: That's right, there were small groups that appeared, and we weren't able to say straightaway whether they were coming in from Kosovo and from Macedonia and whether they infiltrated the border belt from them to open fire at the forces along the border belt which detracted the forces, and this also helped create conditions for groups from Albania, on groups from Albania from infiltrating the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be admitted as Exhibit Number D00575. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have D006-1278 next, please, which is document number 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for that document to appear on our screens, let me say that it is a copy of the Official Gazette. Colonel, we have heard all the problems raised before the higher state organs in the course of November, December, and January -- November December 1998 and January 1999, and we see the problems that have occurred on the basis of this report. The Official Gazette of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on Friday, the 5th of March, 1999, decision on amending the decision defining the border area in certain parts of the state border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Does this decision have anything to do with the events that we witnessed before that?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that on the basis of -- that this decision -- that there was a profound analysis of the situation and the functioning of the state security border system before this decision was written, not only in this area, but in Montenegro and the area facing Macedonia, Bulgaria, Romania, and so on. So these border organs at one of their collegium meetings discussed border proposals and came to the conclusion that the security system needed to be improved and that was the opinion of the expert group set up at the request of the General Staff. So we accumulated all this knowledge, gathered all the knowledge, put it down on paper and saw that the border belt needed to be additionally expanded so as to create the necessary conditions to provide proper security for the border and the country to be able to stand up to external aggression. They weren't only incidents by that time, they were actual acts of aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender into evidence now -- I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit Number D00576. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Now let's look at D574, a Defence document once again. It's the map that we were looking at earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at this map, can you explain to us, and linked to the decision of the 5th of March, 1999 and the establishment of the boarder belt and the amendment to the 21st of July decision, what border belt reflected this March decision? What colour on the map?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: On this map -- well, I can't say which colour but the darker colour anyway. Is it dark pink or is it -- it's not a very clear colour, anyway, the darker area, shaded area, and I'd like to say that this was conditionally speaking an expansion of the border belt, or rather establishing the border belt at a greater depth within the FRY facing Albania and Macedonia. That was the proposal that was submitted to the government, and the government later adopted it. And according to that proposal and decision, the border belt was established in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let's clear one thing up, there were some documents that were mentioned talking about a 5- or 10-kilometre expansion of the border belt. Now, according to the markings here, we see that the depth of the border belt is different at different parts of the border. So what does it mean when we say to establish and fix the border belt? How is that done?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Let me say at the outset that fixing the border belt is something that the highest organs of the government carry out at the proposal of a professional body to ensure that the life and work of the people at the border, the soldiers and everybody else, the MUP and the people in the area are secure or can secure the border crossings. This included the customs services, the customs also had their tasks with respect to the border crossings. So it was fixed at a deeper depth. The border belt was never established at a 5- or 10-kilometre depth. It depended on the facilities and features on the ground, and here, if you look at this map carefully, we see that we avoided having larger settlements such as Djakovica, Prizren, and Urosevac thrown outside the border belt because the object was to ensure normal life for the people in that area, in those larger towns. The others had to stay within the belt so that the security organs could perform their duties properly. And I have to repeat and stress once again, the population living within the border belt where they reside, there was no -- there were no obstacles to these people moving around. All they needed was an ID saying that they were from such and such a village if they were stopped and asked by anybody. Whereas anybody else coming from the hinterland into the border belt had to have extra permission for moving around the border belt. That is the substance of this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have Defence Exhibit 006-1352.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And, Colonel, it is document number 10 in your set. Before the document comes up on our screens, tell me this, please, do you know that the observation mission, observer mission during 1998 and 1999, visited the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, that they were there, and if so what was your relationship with them and how did they, in fact, carry out their work of observation?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that and our relations were, for the most part, well, there was nothing untoward or improper. Conditions were good and we didn't have any problems with respect to their stay and work in the border belt. There weren't any special problems. And at some meetings, they even raised that question, they said they were satisfied with the treatment and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the regime like? What did the members and did the members have to do anything when they entered this border belt, and how were they enabled to go about their duty?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: It was like this: In the border belt, we had some terrible things happening and we've already mentioned some of them today. Now, when it came to the members of the mission, we insisted, the observer mission, we insisted that they had to request and be given permission to move around for the border belt, not for just one day, but for five days, ten day, a month, to have a valid pass and permit to move around the border belt. They had to have this permit so that we could provide security for them in the performance of their duties, and frequently, we were afraid that -- well, we were afraid that they would be fired at and have the border units providing security for the state borders accused of that. So the sole condition was that they had a permit to move around the area, and if they had anything urgent, they could contact the liaison officer allowing them special permits to move around because they might have to visit some observation tower, 20 or 30 kilometres away and not be able to return. So whenever the possibility existed, we would ask them to announce their intentions 24 hours before they needed to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's look at the next document, which is one from the Pristina Corps Command dated the 2nd of March, 1999, and it says there that the representatives of the OSCE expressed their satisfaction with the co-operation they had and the changes in approach to the mission by the organs and units of the Army of Yugoslavia. They pointed out that the problem of access to the border area was resolved and that communication was established between the mission and the liaison officer which guarantees co-operation. They were told that they could submit a seven-day plan of visits that they would then later have to observe, and that they should announce similar visits 24 hours in advance. They accepted that, and this will make it possible for us to prepare and organise ourselves better for access to the border area. Could we please have your comment?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I've already given my comment basically. The essence of this is to truly make it possible for them to be active in the border area as stipulated by the international agreement. So they would submit this plan to the organ who was their host, as it were, in charge of co-operation with them, and then they would make it possible for them to move about so they wouldn't have to make -- wait for this person to come because these people had other things to do as well. For example, the border area, this person cannot sit in his office all the time. He can be moving about. It's a large area after all. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, could it please be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's admitted as Exhibit Number D00577. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat part of your answer. What was the length -- for the transcript. What was the length of the border with Albania?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: No, not with Albania. The length of the border between Albania and Serbia was 332 kilometres and the area of Kosovo and Metohija from Globocica to the tri-lateral border with Macedonia was 127 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have D006-1355. It's number 12 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is the command of the border battalion on the 14th of March. They are submitting this to the Pristina Corps Command, and it says in paragraph 5 in the area of Globocica, three members of the OSCE with a vehicle, et cetera, asked for permission to visit the villages of Gorance, Globocica, Kotlina, Dragomance, and Straza. They were granted permission to visit. So this is the 14th of March. After the border belt was established on the 5th of March, could you please give us your comment how this functioned?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: I cannot see that document here. There is a completely different document under number 10 in my binder but I can say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's 12.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Oh, 12, sorry, I was looking at 10. That's right. Now, this is -- you were asking me about 8.5, yes. It's the area of Globocica. It's the border towards Macedonia. Globocica is actually one of the boarder crossings from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It was Macedonia. There were several towards the Macedonian border, but this is the one that is on the extreme west. There was no impediment for them to work. We just wanted to take the necessary measures to prevent accidents of any kind or heaven forbid something even worse. We wouldn't want any representatives of the international community to be killed in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have this admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's admitted as Exhibit Number D00578. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'd like P1339, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You have it under number 13. Colonel, this is the collegium of the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia on the 18th of May, 1999 -- 18th of March rather, 1999. I would like to have page 18 in English and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 15 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel-General Djordje Curcin provides some information here. I don't want to read it to you. It's rather long. At any rate, it is a meeting held at the request of the head of the OSCE delegation, the 15th of March, 1999, and it was held on the premises of the office for liaising with foreign missions, and you were present as well as Colonel Memisevic and representatives of the first administration. Can you tell us what was discussed and who attending this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: Yes, the meeting was held in Belgrade at the request of Mr. Bo Pelmaz I think his name was, if I'm not mistaken. Bo Pelmaz. This meeting was convened. It so happened that I was sent to attend that meeting. The meeting started and Mr. Bo Pelmaz first asked why the border belt had been expanded and what were the legal regulations that made it possible to do that. Also he asked for permission to move about, or rather, he asked for a document on the basis of which this border belt was expanded. And thirdly, he asked us to give us a map with the broader border belt marked on it. He asked whether that would have any repercussions on the work of the organs of the OSCE. That is to say, whether their work put would have been affected. As I was the professional there who was familiar with the regulations concerned, I responded to his questions saying that the border belt document was adopted in accordance with the law and that such things were done by all countries in the world. Also, I told him as for the decision on the expansion of the border belt, I said to him that we would give him the Official Gazette of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as an official document that will specify exactly where the border belt is. We also told him that he already had a topographic map. I personally saw that he had it. He had a map on a scale of 1:50.000, and his officers could then mark the border belt on that map. Also we added that they could still have unhindered access to the border plan but it was just their duty to provide a plan of their visit. I would also like to add one more thing that Mr. Pelmaz said there and then, that they would not honour that decision. I was surprised. I didn't know how to react. I'm an official, and I know that the laws and regulations of a country have to be respected. Of course, I informed my superiors in Belgrade when I returned about this, and a decision was made that the organs of the MUP and the military organs in charge of the border and representatives of the foreign ministry should convene and discuss the matter. In order to avoid any repetition, all of this was communicated to the foreign ministry, and they took it upon themselves to inform the appropriate organs in the OSCE about what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anything change in relation to the OSCE before and after the border belt was established on the 5th of March, 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK
utterances.text: No, on the contrary, the relations remained the same, and their officials could have unhindered access in the border belt and they could move about freely unimpeded. The only condition was that they announce where they were going and when, but for one sole reason, to make sure that they were provided with the necessary security.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D006-1267. Could we please have that document called up now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am afraid, Mr. Popovic, we'll have to stop you there. I know it's a bit early, but we will continue on Monday. We must adjourn over the weekend now. We continue the evidence on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 8th day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
